context_blocks.text: The selected binary question is the Černý conjecture. Its \((n-1)^2\) upper bound would match the classical worst-case family. A counterexample to the universal bound also answers this card; it need not determine the entire extremal function.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(L(D)=L(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma^{*}\), and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

cards.status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains ordinary two-way determinization as open. Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision supplies a quadratic lower bound, still compatible with polynomial determinization. Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.

context_blocks.text: All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq L\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(L=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

cards.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.

context_blocks.title: Properties should survive renaming
context_blocks.text: A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

context_blocks.title: Why an effective syntax matters
context_blocks.text: One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

context_blocks.title: The known ordered theorem
context_blocks.text: The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

context_blocks.title: Capturing is not one universal time bound
context_blocks.text: One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

context_blocks.title: The remaining gap
context_blocks.text: Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.

cards.title: Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
cards.definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.

context_blocks.text: Every individual term of the sequence is effectively computable from the finite input, and the existence of a zero is semidecidable: positive instances have a finite witnessing index. The unresolved demand is a procedure guaranteed to finish on zero-free inputs too. The problem concerns the whole class of input sequences; undecidability would not mean that the zero question for each particular named recurrence is unanswerable.

The same recurrence describes linear dynamics in \(k\)-dimensional integer space. With \(v_t=(u_t,\ldots,u_{t+k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), let \(B\) have ones just above the diagonal, zeros in the other entries of its first \(k-1\) rows, and last row \((c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1})\). Then \(v_{t+1}=Bv_t\), including when \(k=1\). The question is whether this orbit reaches the hyperplane where the first coordinate is zero. This makes the connection to exact reachability and termination guards in linear programs explicit.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem says that the zero indices form a finite union of arithmetic progressions, together with a finite exceptional set. Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. The card retains arbitrary forward recurrences. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the card. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem on this card.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.

cards.why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.

With \(v_t=(u_t,\ldots,u_{t+k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), let \(B\) have ones just above the diagonal, zeros in the other entries of its first \(k-1\) rows, and last row \((c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1})\). Then \(v_{t+1}=Bv_t\), including when \(k=1\). The question is whether this orbit reaches the hyperplane where the first coordinate is zero. This makes the connection to exact reachability and termination guards in linear programs explicit.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem says that the zero indices form a finite union of arithmetic progressions, together with a finite exceptional set. Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. The card retains arbitrary forward recurrences. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the card. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem on this card.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC.
The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.

Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits \(n^{O(\log ^{2} n)}\) processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.

A negative answer rules out every fixed choice of the size and depth exponents and constants. An algorithm only for bipartite graphs, or one using quasipolynomial circuit size or catalytic auxiliary memory, does not meet the specified positive criterion.

cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge2\), a uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
cards.why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.

cards.definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. Use [synchronous LOCAL rounds](definitions.html#distributed-rounds) with unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.text: The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.

Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
cards.definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.

The question asks whether exact optimization needs a number of arithmetic decisions that grows with numerical precision, or whether the dimensions alone suffice. A positive answer would extend a central efficiency property of several combinatorial optimization problems to every rational linear program.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length. That length can increase while the numbers of variables and constraints stay fixed. Strong polynomiality asks for a dimension-only arithmetic operation count while retaining polynomially bounded numerical representations. It does not promise that writing an arbitrarily long exact output takes a constant number of bit operations.

The three output cases refer to the objective as well as the feasible set. For example, \(x_1=1\), \(x_2\ge0\), with objective \(x_1\), has an unbounded feasible region and finite minimum \(1\). The algorithm must return an optimal vector in this case. Failure to find a feasible point is not by itself a certificate that none exists.

Tardos’s 1986 theorem removes the dependence of the arithmetic operation count on the right-hand side and objective coefficients, while retaining dependence on the constraint matrix. This gives strong polynomiality for important small-coefficient matrix classes. Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver and Végh’s STOC 2024 theorem covers minimum-cost generalized flow and linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, including controlled bit complexity. An unrestricted dense matrix need not belong to these classes.

Allamigeon, Gaubert and Vandame prove exponential iteration lower bounds for interior-point trajectories confined to the specified neighborhoods of self-concordant-barrier central paths. A central path is the curve of minimizers of the barrier-penalized objective as its parameter varies. Their theorem restricts which trajectories the method follows; it is not a lower bound for every arithmetic algorithm for linear programming.

The STOC 2026 trust-region paper gives guarantees relative to the straight-line complexity of an appropriate central-path neighborhood: the number of line segments needed to traverse it. Instance optimality within this path-following framework does not supply a dimension-only polynomial bound on that quantity for every LP. The paper also distinguishes its real-RAM running times from the additional work needed to control bit complexity. Its approximate trust-region subproblems retain accuracy parameters and are not exact general LP solvers.

Awoniyi’s July 2026 revision directly claims a strongly polynomial algorithm for general LP; Lemma 7.1 asserts a linear bound on its iteration count. A separate paper entitled Validation is by the same author, so its title does not establish independent confirmation. This review has not certified the proof or located independent primary validation in bounded searches.

Truffet’s current August 2026 revision also states a general strongly polynomial solution in Theorem 2.1. Its opening revision note acknowledges a logical error in earlier versions and asserts a correction; the current theorem remains a claim requiring verification. This review read that note, the theorem and the stated complexity conclusion, without certifying their proof or the full bit-complexity requirements. These unresolved claims are why the card retains uncertain status.

cards.title: Komlós conjecture
cards.formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}^2\le1\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there exists a single sign vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) for which \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C?\] The constant must be independent of both dimensions and all matrix entries.
cards.definitions: For a real vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), its Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\), and its maximum-coordinate norm is \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The columns \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(A\) may be any vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\le1\), including zero vectors and vectors with negative or irrational entries. The signed sum is \(Ax=\sum_j x_jv_j\), where every one of the \(n\) coefficients is exactly \(-1\) or \(1\). Define the combinatorial discrepancy \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty\); this minimum is attained because there are finitely many sign vectors. The proposition asks for a universal upper bound on this number over all such matrices. The same chosen \(x\) must satisfy every row inequality simultaneously, though it may depend on the full matrix. The column norm bound is individual, not an average across columns; there is no row norm, row-count, rank or sparsity restriction. All matrices are finite, with arbitrary positive dimensions. The task is existence of some finite constant, not determination of the optimal constant and not an algorithm for finding the signs. There is no bit encoding or computational-time restriction on the entries or the sign choice. A fractional vector in \([-1,1]^n\), a vector with unassigned zero coordinates, or independent choices of signs for different rows does not constitute the required witness.

context_blocks.text: Each column represents one choice that can be assigned a plus or minus sign; each row measures the resulting imbalance in one constraint. Euclidean normalization limits the total squared contribution of a single choice across all constraints. The challenge is to control their maximum imbalance with one common assignment. For any fixed matrix the discrepancy is finite; the universal assertion concerns one bound valid for every number of choices and constraints.

If \(B\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is an incidence matrix with at most \(t\ge1\) ones in each column, then \(A=B/\sqrt t\) has column Euclidean norms at most one. A Komlós bound \(C\) would therefore give \(\operatorname{disc}(B)\le C\sqrt t\), which is the Beck–Fiala conjecture. An incidence matrix encodes membership of each of \(n\) elements in each of \(m\) sets. The general real-matrix formulation contains this normalized special case, but does not impose its sparsity or entry restrictions.

Banaszczyk’s 1998 theorem gives the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound in the number of columns. Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s 2019 Theorem 2 gives an efficient randomized algorithm attaining that order. These are full-signing bounds, but their growth with \(n\) leaves the dimension-independent conjecture open. The present card does not add the algorithmic requirement that those stronger constructive results satisfy.

Bansal and Jiang’s original Theorem 1.2 improves the bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\), where the suppressed factors are powers of \(\log\log n\). Their August 2026 exposition states the bound explicitly as \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\). These asymptotic expressions concern sufficiently large \(n\); constants can absorb the finitely many small dimensions. The exponent is one quarter, not four. The bound refutes Hajela’s proposed growing lower bound of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\), but it neither proves nor disproves Komlós’s constant bound.

Ercan’s preprint of 8 September 2026 states, for every admissible \(m\times n\) matrix, \[\operatorname{disc}(A)\le2395\left(1+\log_+(n/9)\right)^{1/4}+2\sqrt2,\qquad\log_+(u)=\max\{0,\ln u\}\quad(u>0).\] This removes the iterated-logarithm factor in the claimed upper bound but still grows with \(n\). The paper reports Lean formalizations with the Bansal–Jiang covariance theorem as an external research-theorem assumption; neither those files nor the new proof were independently verified here. Its existence theorem has no estimated bit-model running time.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s preprint submitted on 10 September 2026 claims the full constant bound: for every admissible matrix, \(\operatorname{disc}(A)<3\sqrt{2\pi}\). Its Theorem 1.1 covers arbitrary real vectors, all positive dimensions and every column norm at most one. If correct, it proves the exact existence target here, and its Corollary 1.2 gives the corresponding Beck–Fiala bound. The authors explicitly make no polynomial-time construction claim. This review checked agreement of the theorem statement with the card, but did not independently verify the complete new proof; the status is therefore uncertain.

As a concrete optimization connection, the ESA 2026 paper by Gribanov and coauthors derives algorithms for integer linear programs whose parameter dependence is expressed using Komlós discrepancy bounds. Its published abstract states that the conjecture would reduce the relevant dependence on the number of constraints to a single exponential, with the other stated input parameters retained. This is a conditional application of the conjecture, not evidence that it has been proved.

cards.why: Komlós asks whether controlling the Euclidean size of each vector is enough to balance all coordinates by signs with a dimension-independent error. This is a central link between vector geometry and simultaneous rounding of linear constraints. It would imply the Beck–Fiala bound for sparse set systems and strengthen discrepancy-based guarantees in optimization.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition with a specified finite real constant \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\) there exist positive integers \(m,n\) and a real matrix \(A\) with all column Euclidean norms at most one, such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there is a row \(i\) satisfying \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\). Equivalently, a negative answer proves that these discrepancies are unbounded; the dimensions and matrix may depend on \(C\), without an efficient construction requirement. A fixed finite lower bound on the necessary constant does not refute the conjecture. A bound that grows with a dimension, a partial coloring, or a result limited to sparse, random or nonnegative matrices does not prove the universal target. No optimization of the positive constant is required.

cards.context:
Each column represents one choice that can be assigned a plus or minus sign; each row measures the resulting imbalance in one constraint. Euclidean normalization limits the total squared contribution of a single choice across all constraints. The challenge is to control their maximum imbalance with one common assignment. For any fixed matrix the discrepancy is finite; the universal assertion concerns one bound valid for every number of choices and constraints.

If \(B\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is an incidence matrix with at most \(t\ge1\) ones in each column, then \(A=B/\sqrt t\) has column Euclidean norms at most one. A Komlós bound \(C\) would therefore give \(\operatorname{disc}(B)\le C\sqrt t\), which is the Beck–Fiala conjecture. An incidence matrix encodes membership of each of \(n\) elements in each of \(m\) sets. The general real-matrix formulation contains this normalized special case, but does not impose its sparsity or entry restrictions.

Banaszczyk’s 1998 theorem gives the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound in the number of columns. Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s 2019 Theorem 2 gives an efficient randomized algorithm attaining that order. These are full-signing bounds, but their growth with \(n\) leaves the dimension-independent conjecture open. The present card does not add the algorithmic requirement that those stronger constructive results satisfy.

Bansal and Jiang’s original Theorem 1.2 improves the bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\), where the suppressed factors are powers of \(\log\log n\). Their August 2026 exposition states the bound explicitly as \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\). These asymptotic expressions concern sufficiently large \(n\); constants can absorb the finitely many small dimensions. The exponent is one quarter, not four. The bound refutes Hajela’s proposed growing lower bound of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\), but it neither proves nor disproves Komlós’s constant bound.

Ercan’s preprint of 8 September 2026 states, for every admissible \(m\times n\) matrix, \[\operatorname{disc}(A)\le2395\left(1+\log_+(n/9)\right)^{1/4}+2\sqrt2,\qquad\log_+(u)=\max\{0,\ln u\}\quad(u>0).\] This removes the iterated-logarithm factor in the claimed upper bound but still grows with \(n\). The paper reports Lean formalizations with the Bansal–Jiang covariance theorem as an external research-theorem assumption; neither those files nor the new proof were independently verified here. Its existence theorem has no estimated bit-model running time.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s preprint submitted on 10 September 2026 claims the full constant bound: for every admissible matrix, \(\operatorname{disc}(A)<3\sqrt{2\pi}\). Its Theorem 1.1 covers arbitrary real vectors, all positive dimensions and every column norm at most one. If correct, it proves the exact existence target here, and its Corollary 1.2 gives the corresponding Beck–Fiala bound. The authors explicitly make no polynomial-time construction claim. This review checked agreement of the theorem statement with the card, but did not independently verify the complete new proof; the status is therefore uncertain.

As a concrete optimization connection, the ESA 2026 paper by Gribanov and coauthors derives algorithms for integer linear programs whose parameter dependence is expressed using Komlós discrepancy bounds. Its published abstract states that the conjecture would reduce the relevant dependence on the number of constraints to a single exponential, with the other stated input parameters retained. This is a conditional application of the conjecture, not evidence that it has been proved.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_c\) and constants \(C_c,K_c\ge1\), \(d_c\ge0\), all integers, with the following guarantee? Every promised input consists of \(n\ge2\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) with \(m\) nonzero entries, a nonzero vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^n\), and an integer \(1\le p\le c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Every input numerator magnitude and positive denominator has at most \(c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) binary digits, and
\[\kappa_2(A)\le n^c.\]
On every run, \(A_c\) must halt within
\[C_c m\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{d_c}\]
word operations in the model below, with word length \(w=K_c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). With probability at least \(2/3\), its explicit rational output \(\widehat x\in\mathbb Q^n\) must satisfy
\[\|A\widehat x-b\|_2\le2^{-p}\|b\|_2.\]
The constants and the finite program may depend on \(c\), but must work for all promised dimensions, matrices, right-hand sides and accuracies. Matrices may be nonsymmetric and indefinite.
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(n,m,p\) in binary, followed by an unordered list of \(m\) triples consisting of a row index, a column index and a nonzero rational value, with distinct positions in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\), and then all \(n\) entries of \(b\). Unlisted matrix entries are zero. Rational numbers are signed binary integer numerators and positive binary integer denominators; reduced fractions are not required. The binary length of zero is one, and a sign is stored separately. Fixed separators specify the list boundaries and integer lengths. Nonsingularity implies \(n\le m\le n^2\), so the total encoding has \(O_c(m\log n)\) bits. The parameter \(c\) specifies the family of promises, rather than an additional runtime input. The algorithm need not verify the promises; guarantees are required only on inputs satisfying them.

For a real vector \(z\), \(\|z\|_2=(\sum_i z_i^2)^{1/2}\). Define \(\sigma_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), \(\sigma_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), and \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). The minimum is positive for nonsingular \(A\). The requested error is relative residual error for this exact rational input, with \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\). It is not a promise that the approximate vector has the same relative forward error as the residual.

The word RAM has a fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of registers, each holding an unsigned \(w\)-bit word. Input is stored as an explicit binary string packed into a read-only word array. Working memory consists of \(w\)-bit cells addressed by \(w\)-bit words and initially zero; no input-dependent advice or precomputed table is supplied. A step performs one read or write, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or logical shift of a word. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Address computations use the same instructions. One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one step. Longer integers occupy multiple cells and use multiple operations. No instruction acts on an arbitrary real number or arbitrary-length integer at unit cost.

The output is a length-delimited explicit list of \(n\) signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Every output word must be written, and all its bits occupy the output encoding. Input processing, preprocessing, any auxiliary matrices, numerical precision, randomness and output cost are included in the stated time bound. The clock is a worst-case bound on every choice of random words, not an expected bound. Probability refers only to the algorithm's independent randomness for each fixed input. An invalid output counts as failure. Uniformity means one program for each fixed \(c\), without dependence on \(n\) or on the particular input; no extra effective procedure generating programs from \(c\) is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its full logical negation, in this word-RAM model. An affirmative proof must establish the algorithm, its worst-case clock and its success guarantee for every fixed \(c\) and every input in the associated promise family. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(c\), no finite program and constants satisfy all these guarantees. It must exclude all algorithms in the stated model, rather than only a chosen iterative method or preconditioner. A result restricted to one structured matrix family, a different output representation or an uncharged real-arithmetic model does not meet the target.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The retained proposition is an explicitly editorial near-linear target, not a named conjecture or the already resolved faster-than-matrix-multiplication question. Inspected primary results improve general polynomial bounds or handle structured families; the August 2026 report retains narrower scalable-solver and finite-precision questions. Bounded later-work searches found no matching universal solver or unconditional impossibility proof. This status assessment does not independently certify the cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: Sparse linear equations are a basic subroutine in optimization and scientific computation. A matrix with \(m\) nonzeros can be stored without its \(n^2-m\) zero entries, and multiplying it by a vector requires only a small amount of arithmetic per stored coefficient. Whether solving the system can have comparable worst-case cost is a stronger question. Moderate conditioning controls numerical sensitivity, but does not itself supply an efficient solver.

Residual error and solution error are different. With \(x^*=A^{-1}b\),
\[\frac{\|\widehat x-x^*\|_2}{\|x^*\|_2}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|A\widehat x-b\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.\]
For example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(b=(1,\delta)\) and \(\widehat x=(1,0)\), for \(0<\delta<1\), have absolute residual \(\delta\) even though the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The card fixes the norm, conditioning and requested tolerance so that these distinct accuracy notions are not conflated.

Spielman and Teng obtain nearly linear expected-time algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant matrices, whose diagonal entries satisfy \(A_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\). Their error guarantee uses the energy norm \(\|z\|_A=(z^{\mathsf T}Az)^{1/2}\). Their paper also analyzes finite precision. For positive-definite inputs, comparison with the Euclidean residual depends on conditioning. These results establish the importance of structural assumptions; their stated norm and expected-time convention are not identical to this card's general guarantee.

Peng and Vempala's SODA 2021 theorem gives a general finite-precision solver that beats matrix-multiplication time for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. The theorem measures residual relative to the projection of the right-hand side onto the column space; for the nonsingular square inputs here, that projection is simply \(b\). The work later appears in JACM in 2025. Asking only to beat the matrix-multiplication barrier would therefore miss the remaining near-linear question.

Nie's 2022 result improves the general bound to
\[\widetilde O\!\left(m^{(\omega-2)/(\omega-1)}n^2\right)\]
in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. Here \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent and \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors. For \(m=\widetilde O(n)\), the displayed bound becomes \(\widetilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})\). This remains well above near-linear time; the historical numerical exponent printed in the paper is tied to the matrix-multiplication bound then available.

Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang show that linear equations in Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes are sparse-linear-equation complete. Their reduction preserves sparsity up to logarithmic factors and has polynomial effects on coefficient sizes, conditioning and requested accuracy for the stated integer-input family. Thus apparently structured higher-dimensional systems already capture substantial general difficulty. This is a reduction between solver tasks, not an unconditional lower bound ruling out a near-linear algorithm.

The August 2026 Simons workshop report discusses scalable solvers for parameterized partial-differential-equation benchmarks, preconditioning, and finite-precision iterative methods. Those questions distinguish guarantees for a selected family from a universal guarantee over sparse inputs. They also distinguish iteration counts from a full cost accounting. The report supplies contemporary context rather than a theorem settling the editorial target here.

The output is part of the computational task. Writing \(n\) approximate coordinates is compatible with near-linear sparse-input time because \(m\ge n\). Returning selected observables, oracle access to an implicit vector, or a quantum state changes that requirement. Requiring the exact rational solution instead would also change the question by introducing potentially much larger coordinate encodings. The stated word model charges storage and processing of all precision actually used.

cards.context:
Sparse linear equations are a basic subroutine in optimization and scientific computation. A matrix with \(m\) nonzeros can be stored without its \(n^2-m\) zero entries, and multiplying it by a vector requires only a small amount of arithmetic per stored coefficient. Whether solving the system can have comparable worst-case cost is a stronger question. Moderate conditioning controls numerical sensitivity, but does not itself supply an efficient solver.

Residual error and solution error are different. With \(x^*=A^{-1}b\),
\[\frac{\|\widehat x-x^*\|_2}{\|x^*\|_2}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|A\widehat x-b\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.\]
For example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(b=(1,\delta)\) and \(\widehat x=(1,0)\), for \(0<\delta<1\), have absolute residual \(\delta\) even though the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The card fixes the norm, conditioning and requested tolerance so that these distinct accuracy notions are not conflated.

Spielman and Teng obtain nearly linear expected-time algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant matrices, whose diagonal entries satisfy \(A_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\). Their error guarantee uses the energy norm \(\|z\|_A=(z^{\mathsf T}Az)^{1/2}\). Their paper also analyzes finite precision. For positive-definite inputs, comparison with the Euclidean residual depends on conditioning. These results establish the importance of structural assumptions; their stated norm and expected-time convention are not identical to this card's general guarantee.

Peng and Vempala's SODA 2021 theorem gives a general finite-precision solver that beats matrix-multiplication time for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. The theorem measures residual relative to the projection of the right-hand side onto the column space; for the nonsingular square inputs here, that projection is simply \(b\). The work later appears in JACM in 2025. Asking only to beat the matrix-multiplication barrier would therefore miss the remaining near-linear question.

Nie's 2022 result improves the general bound to
\[\widetilde O\!\left(m^{(\omega-2)/(\omega-1)}n^2\right)\]
in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. Here \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent and \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors. For \(m=\widetilde O(n)\), the displayed bound becomes \(\widetilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})\). This remains well above near-linear time; the historical numerical exponent printed in the paper is tied to the matrix-multiplication bound then available.

Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang show that linear equations in Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes are sparse-linear-equation complete. Their reduction preserves sparsity up to logarithmic factors and has polynomial effects on coefficient sizes, conditioning and requested accuracy for the stated integer-input family. Thus apparently structured higher-dimensional systems already capture substantial general difficulty. This is a reduction between solver tasks, not an unconditional lower bound ruling out a near-linear algorithm.

The August 2026 Simons workshop report discusses scalable solvers for parameterized partial-differential-equation benchmarks, preconditioning, and finite-precision iterative methods. Those questions distinguish guarantees for a selected family from a universal guarantee over sparse inputs. They also distinguish iteration counts from a full cost accounting. The report supplies contemporary context rather than a theorem settling the editorial target here.

The output is part of the computational task. Writing \(n\) approximate coordinates is compatible with near-linear sparse-input time because \(m\ge n\). Returning selected observables, oracle access to an implicit vector, or a quantum state changes that requirement. Requiring the exact rational solution instead would also change the question by introducing potentially much larger coordinate encodings. The stated word model charges storage and processing of all precision actually used.

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.
cards.why: KLS asks whether covariance normalization alone controls the relation between global variation and local change for every log-concave distribution. Its equivalent geometric expansion principle is central to concentration inequalities and the analysis of random walks used for sampling, integration and convex optimization.
