context_blocks.text: Isotropy fixes scale in every linear direction. For a unit vector \(\theta\), the function \(f(x)=\sum_i\theta_i x_i\) has variance one and gradient energy one, so every admissible universal constant is at least one. The conjecture asks whether nonlinear observables can have an arbitrarily greater variance relative to their average squared local change. Log-concavity is much weaker than independence of coordinates or a uniformly curved smooth potential.

The geometric formulation compares the boundary size of a set with the probability mass it separates. For a Borel set \(S\), let \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\}\), where distance is the infimum of \(\|x-y\|_2\) over \(y\in S\), and define \(\mu^+(S)=\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S))/\varepsilon\). The Cheeger expansion constant is \(h_\mu=\inf_{0<\mu(S)<1}\mu^+(S)/\min\{\mu(S),1-\mu(S)\}\). KLS asserts a positive universal lower bound on this expansion after isotropic normalization. A small value describes a separator with little boundary relative to the masses on its sides.

Notation changes across sources: Lee and Vempala’s survey uses its isoperimetric symbol for expansion itself, while Klartag and Letwin use \(\psi_\mu=1/h_\mu\), the reciprocal. With the latter convention, \(\psi_\mu^2\) and \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)\) differ by at most universal factors for log-concave measures, as recalled in Klartag’s equation (1.4). Thus an upper bound \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) on the reciprocal expansion means an upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) on the Poincaré constant, rather than the same exponent.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks: poor expansion can slow movement between substantial parts of a convex body. The Lee–Vempala survey explains how sampling supports volume estimation, integration and optimization. These algorithmic consequences also depend on access to the input body or density, initialization and the chosen walk; the analytic inequality alone is not a complete computational-cost statement.

Klartag and Lehec’s 2022 Theorem 1.1 gives a polylogarithmic upper bound on reciprocal expansion, with exponent five in that paper. This broke the earlier subpolynomial dimension dependence. It is a historical bound, not a dimension-free resolution.

Klartag’s 2023 Theorem 1.2 improves reciprocal expansion to \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)=O(\log n)\). These logarithmic estimates are stated for \(n\ge2\); no formula involving \(\log1=0\) is asserted for the one-dimensional case.

Klartag and Lehec’s thin-shell paper, first posted in 2025 and revised in February 2026, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le a n\) and consequently \(\mathbb E(\|X\|_2-\sqrt n)^2\le a\) for a universal \(a\) and isotropic log-concave \(X\). These results control particular radial observables. Their relation to the now resolved slicing problem does not turn them into the full inequality for every locally Lipschitz function.

Chen and Klartag’s July 2026 preprint states the sharp radial bound \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le8n\), with equality for independent centered exponential coordinates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 was inspected, but its complete new proof was not independently verified here. This optimizes the thin-shell constant, not the universal Poincaré constant over all test functions.

Letwin’s preprint of 27 July 2026 states \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\le2\mathbb E\|\nabla(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\|_2^2\) for every real symmetric matrix \(M\), where \(X\) is isotropic and log-concave. It derives \(\psi_n=O((\log n)^{1/4})\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(\psi_n=\sup_\mu\psi_\mu\) over the measures in dimension \(n\). Its general-function consequence is \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)=O(\sqrt{\log n})\), which still grows. The paper’s new proof was not independently verified in this review.

Zhang’s sampling preprint, revised on 5 September 2026, still explicitly calls KLS open. It claims an improved mixing theorem for hit-and-run, the walk that chooses a random line through its current point and then a uniform point on the chord inside the body. The result requires a warm initial distribution, whose density is bounded by a finite multiple of the uniform target density, and retains dependence on the KLS constant. Resolving that mixing-time question is therefore distinct from proving a universal Poincaré bound.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a real constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit knot-diagram encoding \(D\) of bit length \(N\), the machine halts within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps and outputs
\[
M(D)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{the knot represented by }D\text{ is ambient isotopic to the unknot}?
\]
It must output zero for every nontrivial knot. The same machine and constants must work for all diagrams, without auxiliary certificates or advice.
cards.definitions:
The \(3\)-sphere is \(S^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_{i=1}^4x_i^2=1\}\), equivalently the one-point compactification of \(\mathbb R^3\). A tame knot is an embedded circle in \(S^3\) that can be carried by an ambient isotopy to a finite polygonal embedded circle in \(\mathbb R^3\). Wild embeddings are excluded.

An ambient isotopy is a continuous map \(H:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3\) such that each \(H_t=H(\,\cdot\,,t)\) is a homeomorphism and \(H_0\) is the identity. Two knots have the same type if some such \(H_1\) takes one onto the other. The unknot is the type of a round planar circle. Knots are not given an orientation.

A knot diagram is a plane drawing of one immersed circle with finitely many transverse double crossings and a choice of overpassing strand at every crossing. The drawing determines a tame knot by separating the two strands locally in the third coordinate. Its input representation is combinatorial, so real coordinates are unnecessary.

For a diagram with \(n\ge1\) crossings, encode a connected graph with \(n\) vertices and four half-edges at each vertex. A half-edge is one end of an edge; an explicitly listed pairing of the \(4n\) half-edges forms the edges. Loops and parallel edges are allowed. At every vertex list the four incident half-edges in cyclic order, and mark which of the two opposite pairs is overpassing. The other pair is underpassing. Also designate one face as the outer face.

The cyclic orders must define a cellular embedding in the sphere: replace each vertex by an oriented disc, join paired half-edges by bands respecting the orders, and cap each resulting boundary circle by a disc. The resulting surface must be a sphere. Equivalently for this connected rotation system, its face cycles must give Euler characteristic \(n-2n+f=2\), where \(f\) is their count. The outer face gives a plane drawing.

Following edges and continuing through the opposite half-edge at each crossing must trace a single unoriented closed component. Thus the representation describes a knot, not a multi-component link. A separate fixed code represents the crossing-free circle. All indices, pairings, cyclic lists and crossing bits are written explicitly in binary with fixed delimiters. They can be checked combinatorially in polynomial time; malformed encodings may be rejected.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing-machine program with finitely many tapes. A step reads and writes a bounded number of tape symbols; arbitrary-length integer operations are not unit-cost operations. It receives no spanning disc, invariant, simplification sequence, random bits, oracle or length-dependent advice. The required output is one bit, not an isotopy or diagram simplification.

cards.status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 v1 claims a deterministic polynomial-time solution. This review examined its statement and main proof dependencies but did not independently establish the local-minimality argument in Lemma 6 or all compressed-update bounds in Lemmas 8–10. No later revision or independent validation was located through 16 September 2026. The card therefore remains uncertain, rather than being declared resolved or unconditionally open. The July hierarchy paper, polynomial certificate theorems and earlier quasipolynomial announcement are recorded with their distinct scopes.

context_blocks.text: A complicated knot diagram can represent a circle that has merely been drawn in an awkward way. The task is to distinguish such projections from actual knots, using a finite description of crossings and planar incidence. No physical model of rope or numerical geometry is involved.

Both positive and negative instances have short efficiently checkable certificates. The NP theorem certifies unknottedness, and the coNP theorem certifies knottedness. These are existence statements about verifiable evidence; they do not show how to find the evidence in deterministic polynomial time.

Thus the problem belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\). Here NP consists of decision problems with polynomial-size witnesses verifiable in polynomial time, and coNP contains their complements. NP-hardness of this particular problem under polynomial-time reductions would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\); a proof that it is outside P would in particular separate P from NP.

Lackenby proves that an unknot diagram with \(n\) crossings admits a simplification using at most \((236n)^{11}\) Reidemeister moves. These are local changes of diagrams that preserve knot type. The theorem bounds a successful sequence’s length, while an algorithm must determine appropriate moves without an uncontrolled search.

The March 2021 Oxford announcement states a recognition algorithm with running time \(n^{O(\log n)}\). The checked SoCG 2025 article still describes that result as announced. Such a quasipolynomial bound allows a growing exponent and therefore does not give the fixed exponent requested here.

The SoCG 2025 factorisation work distinguishes practical performance from worst-case guarantees. It reports that Regina’s recognition algorithm behaves polynomially in experiments despite an exponential worst-case bound. Testing many diagrams cannot establish a bound for every possible input.

Lackenby’s July 2026 hierarchy algorithm gives another recognition method. Section 9 bounds iteration counts by \(L(g+1)^L\), where \(L\) is a hierarchy-length bound and \(g\) bounds surface pattern complexity. These parameters are not bounded there as functions of the original diagram size, and some operation costs also remain unspecified. The displayed iteration estimate is not a polynomial-time theorem for this card.

Musick’s September 2026 preprint claims a positive solution. A bridge presentation separates the knot into trivial arcs in two balls. The preprint claims to find a locally minimal bridge presentation in polynomial time using compressed data, then invokes the fact that a locally minimal presentation of the unknot has one bridge.

The claim’s key dependencies include completeness of the permitted simplifications for local bridge minimality and polynomial manipulation of arc multiplicities. This review read those arguments but did not independently certify them. The scientific status remains uncertain pending validation; no counterexample to the claim is asserted.

cards.title: Planar k-set growth exponent
cards.formal: Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le Cn(k+1)^a\}.\] Here \(K_2(n,k)\) is the largest number of distinct \(k\)-point subsets strictly separable by a line in an \(n\)-point planar set with no three collinear points. Its full definition is below. The bound must be uniform in both integer parameters. Logarithmic factors and exact extremal counts are not requested.
cards.definitions:
For a finite set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
\mathcal S_k(P)=\bigl\{S\subseteq P:\ |S|=k,\ 
\exists(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\ 
\exists t\in\mathbb R:\ 
a x+b y<t\ \forall(x,y)\in S,\ 
a x+b y>t\ \forall(x,y)\in P\setminus S\bigr\}.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), define
\[
K_2(n,k)=
\max_{\substack{P\subseteq\mathbb R^2,\ |P|=n\\
                 \text{no three points of }P\text{ are collinear}}}
|\mathcal S_k(P)|.
\]


The plane \(\mathbb R^2\) has arbitrary real coordinates. A point set contains distinct points. General position here means exactly that no three points lie on one affine line; there is no grid, precision, distribution or convex-position restriction.

The affine line \(a x+b y=t\) has nonzero normal vector \((a,b)\). The strict inequalities in the definition place all points of \(S\) on one side and all other points on the opposite side. In particular the separating line contains no input point. A member of \(\mathcal S_k(P)\) is a k-set. Each subset is counted once, regardless of how many lines separate it.

The maximum is well-defined: every count is an integer between zero and \(\binom nk\), and there are general-position point sets of each permitted size. Thus the set of attained counts is a nonempty finite set of integers even though coordinates range over infinitely many possibilities.

Complementing subsets gives the same count for \(k\) and \(n-k\). Sizes zero and \(n\) each give one subset, so the stated domain captures the nontrivial range. The target is a combinatorial extremal function, not the time complexity of listing k-sets.

In the context, a directed j-edge joins two input points and has exactly \(j\) other points strictly to its left. For even \(n\), an undirected halving edge has \((n-2)/2\) other points on each side of its supporting line. The line through this edge is not a strict separator, since it passes through two points. The requested exponent is \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le C n(k+1)^a\}.\] The integer parameter domain is the same as above. The coefficient \(C\) may depend on \(a\), but not on either parameter or the point configuration. The cited upper bound ensures \(0\le x_{\mathrm{kset}}\le1/3\). The infimum need not be attained. Thus a value zero permits subpolynomial dependence on \(k\) and does not assert a linear bound \(O(n)\). This records the exponent of the dependence on subset size after factoring out the linear dependence on the number of points; it does not assert a two-sided power-law asymptotic.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply \(a\) and prove \(|a-x_{\mathrm{kset}}|\le1/100\) in Lean. For each feasible exponent, one coefficient \(C\) must work for every legal pair \((n,k)\). To exclude an exponent, show that every proposed \(C>0\) fails at some such pair. The infimum need not be attained. A [certified enclosing interval](definitions.html#numerical-answers) of width at most \(1/50\) also suffices via its midpoint.

The 2024 halving-line refinement does not change the upper exponent, and the cited improved halving construction changes a constant in its lower exponent. No matching general bound was found in the bounded review through 16 September 2026; this review does not independently certify all cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: A linear cut realizes only a restricted collection of subsets of a point set. Fixing the subset size measures this restriction more precisely than counting all possible cuts together. The planar problem already exhibits the persistent gap in the broader higher-dimensional question.

For \(k=1\), the separable points are precisely the vertices of the convex hull, the smallest convex set containing \(P\). Their maximum number is \(n\). The unresolved part concerns how the count grows when the selected subset size grows too.

Point-line duality relates these counts to levels in arrangements of lines. A level follows the positions with a prescribed number of arrangement lines below them. Such complexity bounds occur in geometric selection and parametric optimization, where the preferred solution changes with a parameter.

Dey’s general upper bound is \(O(nk^{1/3})\) on the domain of this card. Tóth’s constructions give \(n\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}))\) k-sets. Thus the existing upper and lower estimates do not differ by only a universal constant when \(k\) increases.

In the plane, k-sets correspond to directed \((k-1)\)-edges. For even \(n\), subsets of size \(n/2\) therefore correspond to the two orientations of undirected halving edges. Consequently \(K_2(n,n/2)\) is twice the maximum number of halving edges. The index \((n-2)/2\) counts points on one side of a halving edge, not the size of a halving subset.

Nivasch’s construction gives \(\Omega\!\left(n\exp(\sqrt{\ln4}\sqrt{\ln n})/\sqrt{\ln n}\right)\) halving edges for every even \(n\), with an asymptotically larger exponent constant than earlier constructions. Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This lower-bound expression grows faster than \(n(\log n)^A\) for every fixed \(A\), but slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). These comparisons concern the displayed construction, not a proved upper bound on the unknown optimum.

The 2024 halving-line paper improves lower-order and finite-size terms while retaining the leading four-thirds upper power in the balanced case. Such lower-order changes do not themselves determine the uniform exponent selected here.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
cards.definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.

context_blocks.text: The compressed object lets a fixed decoder reproduce every label in the original training sample. It need not identify the unknown target on points that were never observed. The same decoder must work at every sample size, so a bound depending only on the class’s VC dimension would be independent of how much training data was supplied.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A domain point may require arbitrarily many bits to describe, but sample compression charges one unit for retaining its labeled record. Conversely, an unbounded uncharged message would evade the intended resource bound. Both the retained kernel and the side information are therefore limited explicitly, and the kernel has no free ordering.

Moran and Yehudayoff prove that every binary class of VC dimension \(d\) has a scheme of total size \(2^{O(d)}\). Their sharper theorem also depends on dual VC dimension, which exchanges the roles of domain points and hypotheses by regarding a point as its vector of labels across the class. That dual dimension can grow exponentially in \(d\), leaving the general linear-versus-exponential gap. The checked result is from the corrected v2 and subsequent journal publication.

Chase and coauthors show that some finite classes require an exponential increase in dimension to be contained in an extremal class, a structured type of class with known tight compression. This limits a previously studied embedding-based route to compression. It does not prove that the original class itself requires an exponential-size scheme.

The April 2026 graph-ball paper explicitly retains the general linear conjecture. It gives proper compression of size \(O(t\log(t+1))\) for graph-ball classes whose underlying graph has treewidth at most \(t\), and an analogous cliquewidth result. The predictors are themselves balls, but the resource parameter is graph width and the family is restricted. These structured results are not a universal linear-VC theorem.

The 2025 reduction paper transfers some binary compression bounds to multiclass, regression and robust-learning settings. The sharper transfers need additional reconstruction or stability properties. The ordinary linear conjecture appears in its introduction; its later robust-compression open problem is a different target.

A March 2026 preprint first claimed a sample-compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result. The current checked version, dated 3 August 2026, is withdrawn and identifies an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. Its stale search-result title and earlier abstract are not evidence that the conjecture has been resolved.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that exactly recovers every hidden parity vector from independent uniform examples with independent label noise of rate \(\eta\)? More explicitly, is the following assertion true? \[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/2)\ \exists A_\eta,\ C_\eta,k_\eta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \Pr[A_\eta^{\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}}(1^n)=s]\ge\frac23,\] where every execution takes at most \(C_\eta(n+1)^{k_\eta}\) bit-computation steps, including all example requests and output writing, and \(\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}\) returns a fresh pair \[ (a,b),\qquad a\sim U_n,\quad e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta),\quad b=\langle a,s\rangle\oplus e.\] All vectors, errors and machine coins are independent except for the displayed dependence of each label on its input and the same fixed secret. This retains the existing every-fixed-rate, every-secret search-LPN target.
cards.definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The parity \(\langle a,s\rangle=(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i s_i)\bmod2\) is the XOR of exactly those input coordinates where \(s_i=1\); \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution giving each input vector probability \(2^{-n}\), and \(e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta)\) means \(\Pr[e=1]=\eta\). The secret is arbitrary, fixed before the samples and coins are drawn, and unchanged throughout one execution. Each call returns an independent sample under that fixed secret, including a fresh error bit. The learner may decide when to request more samples based on its previous observations, but cannot choose \(a\), observe the error bit, obtain a clean label, or query a coherent quantum example.

\(A_\eta\) is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using fair independent coins and the specified example oracle. It receives the dimension in unary. The fixed rational rate may be built into the machine; there is no promise that one common algorithm or common exponent works uniformly over rates approaching one half with \(n\). The machine, positive integer constant \(C_\eta\), and positive integer exponent \(k_\eta\) are chosen before \(n\) and \(s\). They may depend on \(\eta\), but have no length-dependent advice. All reading, storing, revisiting examples, computation and output bits are charged; the oracle’s internal sample generation is not charged, and one request costs at least one step. The worst-case bound holds for all possible example and coin histories, not just in expectation. Thus time, samples and stored bits are polynomially bounded, while unrestricted repeated access to stored data is allowed. No single-pass or small-memory constraint is imposed.

The output is exactly one \(n\)-bit vector \(\widehat s\); malformed output is failure. Success means \(\widehat s=s\), not merely low noisy-label error or an unspecified prediction advantage. The probability is over the entire training sample stream and learner randomness for each fixed secret, with no distributional promise on \(s\). Neither \(s\) nor the sample inputs are promised sparse. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The target is the existence of a polynomial-time search procedure, rather than the quantitative size of the best subexponential exponent or a numerical approximation requiring a precision convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or its complete logical negation. A positive result must supply a machine and polynomial resource bound separately for every fixed rational noise rate, and prove exact recovery with the stated probability for every dimension and secret. A negative result must exhibit at least one fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) for which every candidate machine and polynomial bound fail on some dimension and secret, either in the resource guarantee or in recovery probability. Hardness only for a rate depending on \(n\), a restricted statistical-query or small-memory learner, sparse inputs, quantum examples, or under an unproved computational assumption is not the unconditional negation. Recovering a hypothesis with some advantage is sufficient only together with a proved conversion meeting the exact-secret criterion and the same polynomial-resource requirements.

cards.status_note: The checked classical and 2026 primary literature does not provide a matching polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional impossibility for every fixed rational constant noise rate. The May amplification changes parameters; the September worst-case reduction is conditional on a joint code/dual-code hardness premise. The 15 September optical paper’s publisher abstract reports finite structured sparse-constraint experiments, not the stated general guarantee; its full PDF was inaccessible through the publisher gateway. The rate-dependent polynomial convention, classical independent samples and exact every-secret recovery target are retained. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 justify uncertain current status rather than proof of continued openness.

context_blocks.text: Without noise, random parity examples yield a consistent system of binary linear equations. Independent label errors remove that exact algebraic consistency while leaving the hidden rule exceptionally simple. The problem is a standard boundary between efficient noiseless learning and learning with random classification noise.

For every fixed noise rate below one half, \(O_\eta(n)\) examples suffice information-theoretically for exact recovery with constant confidence, although an unrestricted decoder may use exponential computation. The true secret agrees with a fresh noisy label with probability \(1-\eta\); every different parity agrees with probability \(1/2\) under uniform inputs. This statistical separation explains why a polynomial sample bound alone does not settle the computational question.

Collecting sample vectors as matrix rows gives \(b=As+e\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): the columns of the uniform matrix generate a random binary linear code, and the label string is a noisy codeword. Worst-case decoding hardness for arbitrary codes is not itself a hardness proof for this randomly generated sample distribution. The code, noise and sample-count quantifiers matter.

Blum–Kalai–Wasserman give a \(2^{O_\eta(n/\log n)}\)-time algorithm with a comparable subexponential number of examples at fixed noise. They also establish a separation between example-based noise-tolerant learning and statistical-query learning for a restricted parity class. A statistical-query lower bound therefore cannot be treated as a lower bound for every machine that observes individual examples.

Lyubashevsky gives time \(2^{O_{\eta,\gamma}(n/\log\log n)}\) using \(n^{1+\gamma}\) examples for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) in the constant-noise regime. This answers the older subexponential-time polynomial-sample question, but its time remains superpolynomial. Its sample regime must not be silently combined with the faster many-sample BKW exponent.

Garg–Kothari–Liu–Raz prove that noisy-parity learning in their streaming memory model needs either \(\Omega(n^2/(1/2-\eta))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples. Their source uses \(\varepsilon=1/2-\eta\) for the noise bias. At fixed \(\eta\), quadratic memory is permitted by this card, so this unconditional storage lower bound does not exclude the target learner.

Aggarwal–Gupta–Li’s May 2026 paper amplifies success on a small fraction of LPN instances into success on almost all instances with changed dimension and noise parameters. It concerns transformations between hardness and success regimes; it neither constructs a polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed noise rate nor proves that none exists. The parameter changes prevent its abstract from being read as fixed-instance amplification without qualifications.

The September 2026 revision by Aggarwal and coauthors gives conditional low-noise LPN hardness from simultaneous worst-case assumptions about decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 4.1 retain this joint alternative; it is not an unconditional worst-case-hardness theorem for the stated constant-rate search problem.

The publisher abstract of a 15 September 2026 optical-computing paper reports a 512-variable experiment with at most two variables per constraint and numerical comparisons. Those structured sparse constraints and finite physical experiments do not supply the arbitrary-dimension uniform classical polynomial-time guarantee requested here. Only its publisher abstract was accessible during this check.

They also establish a separation between example-based noise-tolerant learning and statistical-query learning for a restricted parity class. A statistical-query lower bound therefore cannot be treated as a lower bound for every machine that observes individual examples.

Lyubashevsky gives time \(2^{O_{\eta,\gamma}(n/\log\log n)}\) using \(n^{1+\gamma}\) examples for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) in the constant-noise regime. This answers the older subexponential-time polynomial-sample question, but its time remains superpolynomial. Its sample regime must not be silently combined with the faster many-sample BKW exponent.

Garg–Kothari–Liu–Raz prove that noisy-parity learning in their streaming memory model needs either \(\Omega(n^2/(1/2-\eta))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples. Their source uses \(\varepsilon=1/2-\eta\) for the noise bias. At fixed \(\eta\), quadratic memory is permitted by this card, so this unconditional storage lower bound does not exclude the target learner.

Aggarwal–Gupta–Li’s May 2026 paper amplifies success on a small fraction of LPN instances into success on almost all instances with changed dimension and noise parameters. It concerns transformations between hardness and success regimes; it neither constructs a polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed noise rate nor proves that none exists. The parameter changes prevent its abstract from being read as fixed-instance amplification without qualifications.

The September 2026 revision by Aggarwal and coauthors gives conditional low-noise LPN hardness from simultaneous worst-case assumptions about decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 4.1 retain this joint alternative; it is not an unconditional worst-case-hardness theorem for the stated constant-rate search problem.

The publisher abstract of a 15 September 2026 optical-computing paper reports a 512-variable experiment with at most two variables per constraint and numerical comparisons. Those structured sparse constraints and finite physical experiments do not supply the arbitrary-dimension uniform classical polynomial-time guarantee requested here. Only its publisher abstract was accessible during this check.

cards.definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability \(1/n^{10}\) still violates the requirement. A probability such as \(2^{- n}\) is negligible, while \(1/n^{10}\) is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(\lambda\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.
cards.why: This asks whether the minimal generic assumption supporting private-key cryptography also supports encryption to a receiver whose encryption key is public. It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

context_blocks.text: Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

cards.context:
Computing a one-way function is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: public information must enable encryption while related private information enables decryption. The question concerns the existence of that additional capability, rather than a performance improvement for a particular deployed scheme.

Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby establish that one-way functions and pseudorandom generators have equivalent existence. A pseudorandom generator deterministically expands a short uniform seed into a longer string that efficient tests cannot distinguish from uniform. Together with the standard consequences surveyed in their conclusion, this supports private-key encryption from one-wayness. Private-key encryption starts from shared secret information, which the present target does not provide.

The target retains the saved one-bit message convention. Public encryptability means an observer can generate its own chosen-plaintext examples, so concealing only a message from an observer denied that capability would be a weaker target. Indistinguishability also requires randomized encryption: a deterministic correct scheme would make the two publicly computable ciphertexts distinguishable. The card permits negligible average decryption error and does not silently impose perfect correctness.

A secure one-bit scheme extends to any prescribed polynomial message length under the same public key, with polynomial loss in correctness and distinguishing advantage. It also implies passive key agreement. General interactive key agreement permits more communication than the two-message interaction associated with public-key encryption, so the related key-agreement card has a separate conclusion. These implications concern existence and security; no additional transmission or authentication task is part of this card.

Impagliazzo and Rudich exhibit an oracle world with one-way permutations but no secure key agreement. Since public-key encryption implies key agreement, the separation also constrains public-key encryption in that world. The original result is from STOC 1989; this audit read the author manuscript dated 28 May 1994. Such a relativized separation does not assert that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary public-key encryption.

Barak and Mahmoody’s corrected April 2009 Theorem 1.1 quantifies the random-oracle limitation: if each party makes at most \(q\) queries and agreement probability is at least \(\rho\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\) an observer can recover Bob’s output with probability at least \(\rho-\delta\) using at most \((16q/\delta)^{2}\) oracle queries. Other computation is unbounded. The paper explicitly corrects an earlier proof and does not extend this quadratic bound unchanged to a random-permutation oracle. It is not a polynomial-time attack on all ordinary encryption schemes.

Chatterjee, Mu and Vasudevan’s EUROCRYPT 2026 construction assumes hardness of planted MinRank on random instances, equivalently a random rank-metric decoding problem. The matrices are random rather than masked members of a specially structured decodable code family. This broadens the available concrete foundations for encryption, but hardness of that specific distribution is not supplied merely by the existence of an arbitrary one-way function. The introduction and definitions were checked in the 2025 preprint; its full security proof was not independently verified.

Li, Ni and Zan’s August 2023 preprint explicitly claims a positive answer from one-way functions. Its statement was checked, but this review has not verified the proof or found a conclusive later assessment. The card therefore records an uncertain scientific status and remains active; neither an accepted resolution nor a refutation of that claim is asserted.

It tests whether the apparent need for additional structure in public-key constructions reflects a true difference in existence or only the known reductions. The distinction controls the foundational assumptions needed for confidential communication without a pre-existing shared secret.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
cards.why: This asks whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable total problems beyond classical randomization. It identifies the exact classical lower bound needed to turn an efficient quantum decision algorithm into an unconditional separation of computational power.

Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. context_blocks.text: Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes on this card still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
cards.why: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation.

progress.text: Aharonov–Arad–Vidick formulate the Hamiltonian conjecture with quantum reductions and explain the reduction qualification in its equivalence to proof checking.

cards.title_en: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions

context_blocks.text: Editorial scope: the existing card explicitly chose deterministic classical reductions. This review preserves that mathematical target and qualifies the title. Aharonov, Arad and Vidick instead state their Conjecture 1.3 under quantum polynomial-time reductions, and explain that permitting quantum reductions is needed for the known equivalence with their proof-verification formulation. The stronger reduction requirement here is therefore not attributed to their conjecture as an established equivalent formulation.

The classical PCP theorem gives constant-gap hardness for constraint satisfaction. Quantum local Hamiltonians replace local Boolean penalties by local operators, while a global state may be entangled across all qubits. The quantum Cook–Levin theorem establishes QMA-completeness at inverse-polynomial relative precision. The constant relative gap asked for here remains an additional claim. The no case rules out low average energy for every state, rather than only product states or a specified family of trial states.

Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe proved the no-low-energy-trivial-states theorem, first announced in 2022 and published at STOC 2023. Their families have bounded-size local interactions and a fixed positive energy-density threshold below which state preparation needs depth \(\Omega(\log n)\). Depth counts layers of disjoint bounded-size quantum gates, with no geometric restriction. This establishes a strong structural phenomenon in low-energy states, but is not a reduction proving QMA-hardness of distinguishing high and low ground energies. In particular, their theorem’s Hamiltonians are frustration-free: they have a common zero-energy state.

The games version also requires care. Natarajan and Nirkhe’s 2024 status note identifies an error in an earlier Natarajan–Vidick energy-amplification argument that invalidates its claimed games PCP for a QMA-complete problem. Their note distinguishes efficient honest provers from arbitrarily powerful entangled provers. Neither the old claim nor general results about interactive games supply the Hamiltonian statement on this card.

Buhrman, Helsen and Weggemans give a detailed quantum reduction between constant-query proof checking and local Hamiltonians, and clarify adaptive-query and multiple-prover variants. Their 2025 theorem controls approximation of a verifier’s acceptance probability by an energy and can produce a fixed classical Hamiltonian description with high probability. The reduction itself is quantum. These structural results do not establish that all QMA problems have constant-query proofs, or that the needed Hamiltonian descriptions can always be computed by classical reductions.

The October 2025 Bergamaschi–Metger–Vidick–Zhang preprint proves a gap-amplification result with an increase in the locality of the resulting Hamiltonian. Its locality-gap tradeoff does not preserve a constant locality throughout the full conjectured gap increase. Thus it is a distinct partial result even though its reductions can be deterministic.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 preprint gives interactive oracle proofs for QMA with polynomial total communication, polylogarithmic query and round counts, and a constant soundness gap. The interaction and nonconstant query bounds are part of the theorem. It does not assert the noninteractive, constant-locality Hamiltonian hardness asked for here. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Nguyen’s July 23, 2026 Simons talk abstract explicitly keeps the general quantum PCP question open and reports amplification of a combinatorial gap. The checked abstract does not assert the full normalized energy-gap theorem. A matching full paper or video proof was not verified in this review.

Bafna and Vyas’s August 19, 2026 preprint also explicitly describes quantum PCP as open. It concerns classical private PCPs for NP, with nonconstant query complexity and additional parameter improvements conditional on a product-expansion conjecture. Its classical result does not verify quantum witnesses or settle this Hamiltonian problem.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).

importance.reason: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation. Editorial placement in this pass: a defining landmark.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every choice of integers \(q\ge2\), \(r,g\ge1\) and real numbers \(J,\Delta>0\), does there exist a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta)\ge0\) with the following property? For every square-lattice size \(L\ge1\), every Hamiltonian satisfying the locality, norm, incidence, unique-ground-state and global-gap conditions below, and every subset \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), its ground state satisfies \[S(\rho_A)\le C\,|\partial A|.\] The constant must be independent of \(L\), the region and the particular interaction matrices. This is an entropy area law for general uniformly gapped two-dimensional local systems.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\Lambda_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^2\), with open boundaries and a copy of \(\mathbb C^q\) at each site. The full Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in\Lambda_L}\mathbb C^q\), with the standard product basis and inner product \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator \(H=\sum_a h_a\), with a finite list of Hermitian interaction terms. Each term acts as identity outside a specified nonempty support \(X_a\subseteq\Lambda_L\). Its support has diameter at most \(r\) in the maximum-coordinate distance \(d_\infty(x,y)=\max\{|x_1-y_1|,|x_2-y_2|\}\). A one-site support has diameter zero. Each site belongs to at most \(g\) listed supports; terms with equal supports are counted separately. Every term has operator norm at most \(J\), where \(\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|\) and \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\). The terms need not be positive, commute, be translation invariant or admit a common energy-minimizing state.

List the eigenvalues of \(H\), with multiplicity, as \(E_0\le E_1\le\cdots\). Its lowest eigenspace is required to have dimension one and \(E_1-E_0\ge\Delta\). Choose a unit eigenvector \(\psi\) for \(E_0\). Uniqueness means uniqueness up to global phase, so \(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) is uniquely specified. The gap condition concerns the entire Hamiltonian only. No lower gap bound is assumed for subregions or subsets of its interaction terms. Both \(J\) and \(\Delta\) are in the same fixed energy units.

For \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), let \(A^c=\Lambda_L\setminus A\) and let \(\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{A^c}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\). Partial trace is defined in product-basis indices by \[(\rho_A)_{u,v}=\sum_z\psi_{(u,z)}\,\overline{\psi_{(v,z)}},\] where \(u,v\) index basis configurations on \(A\), \(z\) ranges over configurations on \(A^c\), and tuples are placed in the original site order. This is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. If its eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\), its entropy in bits is \(S(\rho_A)=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\).

The geometric boundary \(\partial A\) consists of unordered nearest-neighbor lattice edges \(\{x,y\}\) with exactly one endpoint in \(A\), where \(|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|=1\). Its cardinality is measured in lattice units and is defined by geometry, even if a particular Hamiltonian has no term crossing an edge. No exterior vertices or periodic wrap-around edges are added. Regions may be disconnected or touch the exterior boundary. Empty and full regions have zero entropy and zero internal boundary. The interaction matrices may have arbitrary complex entries and may vary with location and with \(L\). There is no finite input encoding, state-preparation task, efficient computation requirement or frustration-free assumption. The question asks for a uniform mathematical entropy bound across all the specified finite systems.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal statement with the displayed order of quantifiers, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative answer fixes one choice of \(q,r,g,J,\Delta\) and shows that for every finite \(C\ge0\), there is an admissible system and region violating the bound. Equivalently, it may exhibit a sequence with these same fixed local parameters, unique ground states, gaps at least \(\Delta\), and unbounded ratios \(S(\rho_A)/|\partial A|\) on nontrivial regions. Allowing the gap to close, the interaction norm or local dimension to grow, or the lowest eigenspace to become degenerate does not refute this statement. A positive result for frustration-free or locally gapped systems, only one family of interactions, or an entropy bound with an unbounded extra logarithmic or subpolynomial factor does not prove it. No algorithm for finding the ground state is required. The statement is an exact yes/no bound; a fixed additive approximation to individual entropies is not a substitute.
