context_blocks.text: A region containing \(m\) sites has entropy at most \(m\log_2q\). For a square block with side length \(\ell\), this volume bound is quadratic in \(\ell\), while the conjecture permits only a constant times its boundary length. Fixing both interaction norms and the gap prevents rescaling an increasingly gapless family from appearing uniformly gapped.

Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped one-dimensional local systems. An interval has only a constant number of boundary edges, so its entropy stays bounded as the chain grows. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not give a constant independent of width: each grouped site has dimension \(q^L\).

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.
cards.why: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.

context_blocks.text: A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

Uniform invariance requires one map \(u:\omega^2\to\omega^2\) that converts any pair of indices witnessing \(x\equiv_T y\) into a pair witnessing \(f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\), independently of the reals. Even this index map is not required to be computable in the survey’s definition. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the two parts for the uniform subclass. Ordinary invariance does not supply such a map.

The regressive case is already settled: if invariant \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq_T x\) on a cone, then on a cone it is constant in degree or equivalent to the identity. Order preservation is a different restriction, namely \(x\leq_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq_T f(y)\). The saved full target includes neither restriction. Earlier extraction of only a regressive subcase was corrected before this audit; this review preserves the full conjecture.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and for all measure-preserving invariant functions. Here the latter means \(\forall a\;\exists b\;\forall x\geq_T b:\ a\leq_T f(x)\), with the base allowed to depend on the fixed target degree. Their Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.8 use determinacy and dependent choice for reals, which follow from this card’s stronger fixed background. The older Part II theorem for order-preserving functions retains a Borel restriction; Borel means inverse images of open sets belong to the sigma algebra generated by the finite-prefix open sets of Cantor space.

The background cannot be replaced by \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). Lutz and Siskind’s §6.4 supplies choice-based counterexamples, including an invariant order-preserving function that is neither constant nor above the identity on a cone. These do not satisfy the determinacy setting. A faithful proof-assistant treatment must keep that internal set universe distinct from any ambient use of choice.

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey withdraws Theorem 1.8, an asserted equivalence whose argument fails at limit ordinals. This audit therefore uses the actual two-part conjecture and checked restricted theorems, without importing the withdrawn equivalence as a fact about arbitrary invariant Borel functions.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision studies conditional consequences of an unresolved decomposition question for Turing equivalence, including nonuniformity for functions whose outputs are compared by many-one reducibility. These are related structural results with a different output reducibility and an additional open premise. They do not claim a counterexample to the full conjecture stated here.

Walsh’s March 2026 journal survey states the full conjecture explicitly as open and distinguishes the order-preserving Part I theorem from the Borel order-preserving Part II theorem. This supplies a dated status source; the bounded September follow-up search is recorded separately from verification of the underlying proofs.

cards.context:
A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

Uniform invariance requires one map \(u:\omega^2\to\omega^2\) that converts any pair of indices witnessing \(x\equiv_T y\) into a pair witnessing \(f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\), independently of the reals. Even this index map is not required to be computable in the survey’s definition. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the two parts for the uniform subclass. Ordinary invariance does not supply such a map.

The regressive case is already settled: if invariant \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq_T x\) on a cone, then on a cone it is constant in degree or equivalent to the identity. Order preservation is a different restriction, namely \(x\leq_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq_T f(y)\). The saved full target includes neither restriction. Earlier extraction of only a regressive subcase was corrected before this audit; this review preserves the full conjecture.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and for all measure-preserving invariant functions. Here the latter means \(\forall a\;\exists b\;\forall x\geq_T b:\ a\leq_T f(x)\), with the base allowed to depend on the fixed target degree. Their Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.8 use determinacy and dependent choice for reals, which follow from this card’s stronger fixed background. The older Part II theorem for order-preserving functions retains a Borel restriction; Borel means inverse images of open sets belong to the sigma algebra generated by the finite-prefix open sets of Cantor space.

The background cannot be replaced by \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). Lutz and Siskind’s §6.4 supplies choice-based counterexamples, including an invariant order-preserving function that is neither constant nor above the identity on a cone. These do not satisfy the determinacy setting. A faithful proof-assistant treatment must keep that internal set universe distinct from any ambient use of choice.

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey withdraws Theorem 1.8, an asserted equivalence whose argument fails at limit ordinals. This audit therefore uses the actual two-part conjecture and checked restricted theorems, without importing the withdrawn equivalence as a fact about arbitrary invariant Borel functions.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision studies conditional consequences of an unresolved decomposition question for Turing equivalence, including nonuniformity for functions whose outputs are compared by many-one reducibility. These are related structural results with a different output reducibility and an additional open premise. They do not claim a counterexample to the full conjecture stated here.

Walsh’s March 2026 journal survey states the full conjecture explicitly as open and distinguishes the order-preserving Part I theorem from the Borel order-preserving Part II theorem. This supplies a dated status source; the bounded September follow-up search is recorded separately from verification of the underlying proofs.

benchmark_focus.reason: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow define propositional proof-system efficiency and formalize the extension rule. Their equivalence theorems make EF polynomial boundedness independent of standard presentations; Cook’s posted correction to Corollary 4.7 keeps the coNP-versus-NP premise explicit.

Wigderson’s book lists superpolynomial unrestricted Frege lower bounds as open and distinguishes the additional sharing available in Extended Frege. Lower bounds for the weaker system would not automatically apply to EF.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) with additional formal provability hypotheses. The checked preprint does not give an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh, Jain, Li and Mathialagan construct succinct non-interactive arguments for NP under promise derandomization, LWE, SXDH and a bounded-arithmetic hardness-certification assumption. The formal unprovability premise differs from the unconditional proof-size target.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations and explicitly explains why it does not give a Frege or EF lower bound for propositional tautologies.

Akbar Tabatabai reports exponential separations between EF systems for intuitionistic substructural and linear logics. The preprint’s stated scope differs from this classical system; its proof was not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). Cook’s author page corrects the premise of Corollary 4.7 in the original paper to coNP differing from NP; a P-versus-NP separation alone is not the stated premise.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

The use of classical implication matters. Recent lower bounds for Extended Frege systems of intuitionistic or linear logics concern different rules and valid formulas. The August 2026 preprint on those systems therefore cannot be read as a solution of the unrestricted classical problem fixed here.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.
Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width \(q\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\) but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions:
Use the shared [bounded-width CNF encoding and rate \(s_q\)](definitions.html#sat-encoding). The exponential term uses the number of distinct variables \(n(F)\). The polynomial factor uses the full input length \(N(F)\), including every repeated clause. The decider may depend on the fixed width \(q\).

The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(N(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected \(\varepsilon\). There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm{P}.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). The deterministic program and its fixed time bound may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or length. All input access, arithmetic and output count in the [bit model](definitions.html#bit-model).

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm{P}.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.

context_blocks.text: A randomized answer is allowed to be wrong with probability at most one third on any specified input. For example, correctness on 99% of all strings of each length would still fail this definition if a remaining string were always answered incorrectly. The uncertainty belongs to the machine’s internal choices, not to which inputs the user may supply.

Adleman’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) allows a separate polynomial-size Boolean circuit at each input length, without requiring one efficient procedure that constructs these circuits. This is a nonuniform existence statement; the target requires one finite deterministic program for all lengths.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove a conditional equality: if a Boolean function computable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) has worst-case circuit complexity at least \(2^{\varepsilon n}\), for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\), then \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\). Circuit complexity here counts gates of unrestricted nonuniform Boolean circuits over a fixed complete finite basis that compute the function correctly on every input of that length. The exponential lower-bound hypothesis is part of the theorem; this is not an unconditional equality or a theorem assuming only \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman’s May 2026 preprint obtains finer conditional derandomization bounds for algorithms with a specified insensitivity property. For each fixed input, changing one uniformly chosen coin coordinate of a correct tape must rarely make the answer incorrect. Their two-sided version additionally constrains incorrect tapes that have a correct neighbor. Theorem 9.10 retains explicit circuit-hardness, insensitivity and error assumptions; these structural conditions are not properties required of every BPP program. The paper distinguishes hitting-set and pseudoentropy generators from general pseudorandom generators.

Tianrong Lin’s July 2026 revision states a direct claim of \(\mathrm{P}\subsetneq\mathrm{BPP}\) in Theorem 1.1, with additional claimed separations. That would answer this card negatively if its proof were valid. This review read the claimed theorem and checked its version history, but has not certified its proof or located independent primary validation in the bounded searches. It is therefore recorded as an unverified claim, and the card retains uncertain status.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. Use [FPT and FPT many-one reductions](definitions.html#parameterized). Here the parameter is the requested clique size \(k\). The languages reducible to this parameterized Clique problem form \(\mathrm{W}[1]\). Hence an FPT algorithm for Clique is equivalent to \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

progress.text: The textbook specifies parameterized reductions and proves the completeness framework for Clique, via its complement relation with Independent Set. Theorem 14.21 derives the stronger exclusion of \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms assuming ETH.

Bottesch identifies the FPT-versus-W[1] separation as the central conjecture, explains its known implications relative to P versus NP and ETH, and proves structural results with explicitly specified oracle conventions. These do not prove the unrelativized separation.
Lin gives a gap reduction showing that a constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique would imply an exact FPT algorithm. The consequence remains conditional on FPT differing from W[1].

Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit and Liu give a combinatorial proof of the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized inapproximability consequence under W[1]-hardness. The checked August 2024 revision precedes the SOSA 2025 publication.

Abboud, Fischer and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique bounds by logarithmic factors. Their August 2024 author revision retains a polynomial exponent depending on k; the institutional record lists the Algorithmica publication on 22 May 2026.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\), there exists an integer \(q\ge2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish the following two classes of explicitly listed Unique Games instances over the alphabet \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\):
\[\text{YES: }\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad \text{NO: }\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta.\]
NP-hardness here means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT with the completeness and soundness guarantees defined below. The alphabet size and the reduction may depend on the two constants but must be fixed before the input size grows. The target is this hardness proposition itself, without assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
cards.definitions:
Instance and value. An instance has a finite vertex set \(V=[n]\) with \(n\ge2\), an ordered nonempty list of \(m\ge1\) directed edges \((u_j,v_j)\) with distinct endpoints in \(V\), and a permutation \(\pi_j:[q]\to[q]\) for each edge index \(j\in[m]\). Repeated directed edges, including repeated constraints or different constraints on the same ordered pair, are allowed and counted separately. There is no restriction on degree, expansion, connectedness or bipartiteness, and isolated vertices are allowed. A permutation is a bijection: each label occurs exactly once among its \(q\) images. A labeling is one map \(\ell:V\to[q]\), with no probabilistic or quantum strategy. Edge \(j\) is satisfied when \(\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\). Define
\[\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_{\ell:V\to[q]}\frac{|\{j\in[m]:\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\}|}{m}.\]
The finite maximum is attained and lies in \([0,1]\). All edge occurrences have equal weight. Reversing an edge would require using the inverse permutation; its stored direction fixes the equation used here. The two promised classes are disjoint because \(\delta<1-\varepsilon\). Instances with \(\delta<\operatorname{val}(G)<1-\varepsilon\) are outside the promise.

Explicit encoding. Vertex labels and all integers are written in binary with length prefixes. Concretely, a nonnegative integer \(z\) may be encoded by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). A game encoding lists \(q,n,m\), all \(n\) vertex labels in order, and for each edge its two endpoints followed by the entire table \(\pi_j(1),\ldots,\pi_j(q)\). Tables are not circuits or oracles representing longer objects. Input and output lengths count every listed bit. This convention fixes a finite-string model; polynomially interconvertible standard explicit encodings give the same hardness question.

Reduction and source problem. A 3CNF formula \(\varphi\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each an ordered disjunction of three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable \(x_i\) or its negation. Repeated literals are allowed. List the variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_s\) and the clauses, recording literal signs as bits and indices and list lengths with the integer encoding above. The empty conjunction is allowed and is true. A satisfying assignment is a map from these variables to \(\{0,1\}\) making every clause true. Let \(|\varphi|\) be the full bit length of this encoding. For fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta,q\), the required reduction is a single deterministic Turing-machine program \(F\) for which some constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) bound its time by \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\) on every valid formula. Time includes writing the output. On each such formula it must output one valid game \(G=F(\varphi)\) over exactly \([q]\), satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\le\delta.\]
Thus both kinds of formulas map into the promise. A multi-tape deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes suffices as the computation model; each transition reads and writes one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. No advice, randomness or oracle is allowed. Behavior on malformed formula strings is immaterial. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is the meaning of NP-hardness used here; no decision algorithm for the game is part of the requested reduction.

Parameter quantifiers. The order is \(\forall(\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists q\ \exists F,C,k\ \forall\varphi\). The machine, alphabet, time exponent and constant may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but not on the formula. The parameters are not growing input variables, and no common polynomial exponent or effective procedure selecting reductions for all parameters is additionally required. Restricting the gap parameters to positive rationals loses none of the usual real-parameter conjecture: smaller rational errors give the required inclusions of the real-parameter YES and NO classes. The usual one-error formulation is equivalent by taking the smaller of the two errors.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the entire quantified hardness proposition, including the deterministic reductions, polynomial output/time bounds, valid permutation constraints, and both implications for every formula, or prove its logical negation. A negative answer must identify fixed rational \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\) such that no alphabet \(q\ge2\) admits the required reduction. Equivalently, for each \(q\) and every deterministic polynomial-time candidate program, some valid 3CNF formula has an invalid output or violates its applicable YES/NO guarantee. This is a statement about all reductions, not just a failed construction or a particular alphabet. No unproved complexity assumption may replace the requested conclusion. A polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm alone does not logically refute the NP-hardness proposition without an appropriate separation such as \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Hardness with completeness bounded away from one, perfect satisfiability testing, a restricted graph class, or a result for many-to-one constraints does not by itself settle this target.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute \(\alpha >0\), an \(\exp (q n^{\varepsilon ^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm finding a \((1- \varepsilon ^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling in a \((1- \varepsilon )\)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-\(\varepsilon\) regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness \(1/2\) and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.
Yoshida reports a sublinear-query tolerant tester with the additional condition \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\); this is not the unrestricted fixed-gap UGC regime.

Fei–Minzer–Wang claim perfect-completeness hardness for 4-to-1 games and consequent coloring hardness. Their introduction still separates full UGC as a conjecture; no independent certification of the new proof is asserted here.

context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally reversible: either endpoint label fixes exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Despite this simplicity, the conjecture asks whether an almost perfectly consistent collection is NP-hard to distinguish from one for which every labeling violates almost all constraints. This is a promise decision gap, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum.

For example, with two labels an identity permutation asks for equal labels, while a transposition asks for different labels. Three transposition constraints on the edges of a triangle have value \(2/3\). This illustrates how individually consistent requirements can conflict globally; the conjecture quantifies over larger alphabets and much more extreme gaps.

Exact satisfiability, meaning \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\), is polynomial-time decidable in this explicit model. The positive completeness error \(\varepsilon\) is therefore an essential feature of the conjecture. A uniformly random labeling satisfies an expected fraction \(1/q\) of the edges, so every instance has value at least \(1/q\). In particular, if \(\delta<1/q\), there are no NO instances. The alphabet cannot be fixed in advance of all soundness thresholds.

Raghavendra’s 2008 theorem ties Unique-Games-based hardness to a general semidefinite-programming framework for constraint satisfaction over a fixed finite domain. Under UGC, its approximation guarantees are optimal up to arbitrary fixed accuracy, with the usual consequence for polynomial-time algorithms requiring a complexity separation. This explains why one apparently narrow family of permutation constraints governs many approximation thresholds.

Arora, Barak and Steurer’s 2010 theorem gives, for an absolute \(\alpha>0\), an \(\exp(qn^{\varepsilon^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm returning a \((1-\varepsilon^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling on an \(n\)-vertex, \((1-\varepsilon)\)-satisfiable instance. For fixed \(q\) and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\), this is subexponential but does not give polynomial time. Its dependence on completeness is compatible with reductions whose polynomial exponent depends on the desired gap.

The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies that, for every fixed positive soundness threshold, Unique Games is NP-hard with completeness \(1/2\). Khot’s exposition states this as Theorem 2.20. The conclusion leaves the near-one completeness in UGC unresolved. The 2025 journal publication of one part of the proof sequence records the historical role of its conditional intermediate theorem and still states full UGC separately as Conjecture 1.4.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims the \(4\)-to-\(1\) Games Conjecture with perfect completeness. Its constraints are projections in which each right-hand label has four preimages, rather than bijections. Theorem 1.6 is a major related hardness claim, with graph-coloring consequences, but does not prove the permutation-constraint UGC. The same introduction retains UGC as Conjecture 1.4 and identifies completeness \(1/2\) as the existing Unique Games hardness frontier. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Yoshida’s May 2026 tolerant-testing preprint concerns adjacency-list queries and distinguishes small from larger optimum violation fractions. Its Theorem 1.1 requires \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\), where \(\rho\) is the larger violation threshold and \(c_q>0\) depends on the fixed alphabet. For the UGC gap, \(\rho=1-\delta\); the displayed assumption does not hold for every input size when the positive errors and alphabet are fixed. Thus the tester’s sublinear query bound does not refute this fixed-parameter, all-instance hardness statement.

cards.title: Deterministic k-server conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite or infinite metric space \((M,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points, and every initial configuration \(C_0\in M^k\), do there exist a deterministic online rule \(A\) and a finite \(\beta\ge0\) such that \[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma;C_0)\le k\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\] for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\)? Both parties have exactly \(k\) servers and start at \(C_0\); movement cost is the sum of distances in the model below. The rule and additive constant may depend on the metric and initial placement, but not on the future requests.
cards.definitions:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), define the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. 

A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each \(k\), metric and initial configuration, a deterministic online rule and a finite additive constant give the stated \(k\)-competitive bound on every sequence. To refute it, fix one such setting and defeat every rule and additive constant.

progress.text: Manasse–McGeoch–Sleator establish the deterministic lower bound \(k\), the two-server case and the \((k+1)\)-point case.
Chrobak–Larmore obtain \(k\)-competitiveness on tree metrics.
Koutsoupias–Papadimitriou establish the general \(2k-1\) deterministic upper bound. The inspected author-hosted manuscript is dated 22 May 1995.
Huang–Zhang prove the three-server circle theorem; their canonical-certificate limitation has a separate restricted scope.
Bubeck–Coester–Rabani's preprint, published at STOC 2023, disproves the randomized logarithmic conjecture with a squared-logarithmic lower bound.
ISAAC publishes a \(2k-1\) lower bound for the time-optimal variant. Its maximum-movement objective differs from the classical sum-of-distances objective.
The potential-discovery benchmark retains the general deterministic conjecture and records the limits of its finite experiments.
ICALP publishes polynomial-time randomized algorithms and a separate advice-assisted consequence, retaining their additional randomness or input.

A new preprint claims that the work-function algorithm is \(k\)-competitive on every metric, with an explicit sequence-independent additive term. If correct, its Theorem 1.2 and the classical lower bound determine \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) exactly. The claim is not independently verified here.

context_blocks.text: On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. As the classical bound before the September 2026 claim, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The selected target is the classical conjecture asserting an actual \(k\)-competitive rule. It implies \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\), but an infimum value alone need not give endpoint attainment. The September 2026 preprint claims the actual competitiveness statement; its proof-review caveat is retained below.

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. It explicitly distinguishes passing those finite checks from a proof covering all configurations and request sequences. Its reported experiments do not resolve the remaining general case.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 theorem gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on \(n\)-point metrics. Its reduction uses few random bits, but does not eliminate randomness. A separate deterministic consequence supplies advice that depends on the instance. Neither extra input nor randomization is present in this card, so these computational improvements do not determine its universal deterministic ratio.

Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński's preprint submitted on 14 September 2026 states in Theorem 1.2 that, for every metric and every finite request sequence,
\[\operatorname{WFA}_{C_0}(\sigma)\le k\operatorname{OPT}_{C_0}(\sigma)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}d(s_i,s_j).\]
Here \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) are the initial server locations. The additive term is finite and depends only on the initial placement, as permitted here. The paper explicitly handles coincident positions with distinct location labels and a pseudometric, and states the theorem for any metric space. Its lazy implementation agrees with the serving convention of this card. The matching claim changes the current status to uncertain pending verification; this review has not independently certified the whole proof.
