cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

cards.status_note: No unconditional proof or unrestricted polynomial-time refutation of this exact fixed-size, balanced constant-success hypothesis was located in a bounded check through 14 September 2026. The cited sum-of-squares theorem is a relaxation/refutation lower bound; the optimal-advantage and September 2026 topology results are conditional, and several newer recovery results use other random graph models. Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

cards.context:
The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

benchmark_focus.reason: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\), and every integer \(q\ge\Delta+2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper labelled \(q\)-colourings satisfies \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^c?\] The constants must be independent of the graph, its degree and the number of colours. This retains the previously selected degree-uniform polynomial target; the time unit is one vertex update, not a sweep or a bit operation.
cards.definitions:
Let \(V(G)=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E(G)\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or parallel edges. Set \(N_G(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\) and \(\Delta=\max_v|N_G(v)|\). The state space is \[\Omega_{G,q}=\{\sigma:[n]\to[q]:\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E(G)\},\] where \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Colours are labelled and may be unused. There is no constraint on colour-class sizes, and no prescribed partial colouring or vertex-specific list. The state space is nonempty for the stated colour range.

At each discrete step, choose \(v\) uniformly from \([n]\). Given the current state \(\sigma\), form the available set \[A_\sigma(v)=[q]\setminus\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}.\] Choose a colour uniformly from \(A_\sigma(v)\), assign it to \(v\), and leave every other vertex unchanged. The set has at least \(q-\Delta\ge2\) elements and includes the current colour; staying in the same colouring is allowed. The choices at successive steps are made from these conditional distributions. Let \(P\) be the resulting finite stochastic matrix and let \(P^t(\sigma,\tau)\) be its \(t\)-step transition probabilities, with \(P^0\) the identity matrix. The chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi(\sigma)=1/|\Omega_{G,q}|\), the uniform law on all proper labelled colourings. In this range it is irreducible and has self-loops, so that this stationary law is approached from every state.

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\), over every proper initial colouring. Denote it by \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\). The chain is ergodic in the stated range.

A step updates one vertex. No factor of \(n\) is absorbed into the time unit, and uniform sampling from a potentially large colour set is part of the mathematical transition rule. Thus the statement concerns the convergence rate of a specified chain, not an implementation bound polynomial only in \(n\) for operations on \(\log q\)-bit colour names. If a graph is encoded for formalization, use its explicit vertex and edge lists and the binary integer \(q\); no succinct graph representation is intended.

The bound is simultaneous for all finite degrees and all \(q\ge\Delta+2\), including \(q\) unbounded as a function of \(n\). A theorem of the form \(C_{\Delta,q}n^{c_{\Delta,q}}\) for each fixed pair of parameters does not automatically meet it. No girth, treewidth, chordality, planarity, expansion or random-graph assumption is imposed. Girth is the shortest cycle length, with infinity for a forest. A fixed multiplicative slack \(q\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\), with \(\delta>0\), does not cover \(q=\Delta+2\) uniformly as \(\Delta\) increases.

The heat-bath convention differs from proposing a uniformly random colour from all \([q]\) and rejecting a conflict, often also called Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. In the heat-bath chain, every proposed colour is available; in the latter chain, unsuccessful proposals contribute further holding probability. Flip dynamics can recolour an entire two-colour component and is a third chain. Related results must retain their update convention and comparison costs. The present question fixes the heat-bath chain exactly.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed uniform polynomial bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its failure. An affirmative proof must supply absolute \(C,c\) working for every graph, degree, colour count and initial proper colouring in the definition. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(C,c\) there are eligible \(n,G,q\) with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)>Cn^c\); one slow instance does not refute every polynomial. Polynomial mixing only for each fixed degree with an uncontrolled exponent, larger multiplicative palette slack, restricted graphs, a different dynamics, or an unspecified faster sampler is not the required bound. This is an exact asymptotic proposition about the specified chain, not a request to approximate a finite mixing time to the numerical benchmark tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The source poses polynomial mixing at the degree-plus-two threshold. This card retains the already adopted heat-bath update rule and the explicit requirement of one polynomial for all degrees and palettes. The source’s initial update description uses proposal-and-rejection; that clock is stated separately rather than silently identifying its transition matrix with this one.

At one fewer colour, a clique on Δ+1 vertices can be frozen: every vertex already sees every other colour. Thus ergodicity itself can fail at q=Δ+1. At q≥Δ+2 the basic chain is ergodic, but eventual convergence alone supplies no polynomial bound on how long it takes.

The2020 source proves polynomial mixing for bounded-treewidth graphs at the additive threshold and for chordal graphs with fixed multiplicative slack. Its treewidth-dependent exponent and the extra hypotheses do not establish the all-graph uniform statement.

The2024 flip-dynamics theorem applies for Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ. Its comparison gives polynomial Glauber mixing in that range; the sharper O(n log n) corollary permits a constant depending on degree and palette. Neither the larger palette ratio nor that parameter dependence is the selected degree-plus-two theorem.

The August2026 girth-seven revision treats Metropolis updates with q≥(1+δ)Δ, for fixed δ and degree sufficiently large in terms of δ. The separate girth-five preprint gives a heat-bath theorem under analogous fixed-slack and large-degree conditions. The latter’s general bound is Oδ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); its optimal-order corollary has further bounded-degree qualifications. Both retain structural assumptions absent here.

The ICALP2026 paper repeats the ordinary colouring-sampling conjecture before studying prescribed colour-class sizes. Fixing class sizes changes the stationary state space and the allowed moves, so those refined sampling results do not settle the chain defined here.

cards.title: FP versus #P
cards.formal:
Is every function in \(\#\mathrm{P}\) computable exactly in deterministic polynomial time? With the numerical function convention defined below, the proposition is
\[\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N},\]
equivalently \(\#\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). Each function may have its own fixed machine and polynomial running-time bound. The output is the exact nonnegative integer in binary.
cards.why: This is the fundamental exact-counting analogue of P versus NP. It asks whether every efficiently checkable family of witnesses also admits efficient evaluation of its full multiplicity, and connects counting satisfiability, permanents and many discrete partition functions under one computational boundary.
cards.status_note: The January 2007 draft and the checked 2017 primary teaching sources pose the exact-counting equality as open. Bounded source searches through 16 September 2026 found no verified proof of either equality or inequality. A March 2026 preprint claiming only the conditional P = NP implication is discussed on TCS-6821; it neither asserts this unconditional equality nor supplies a valid resolution in the local proof check recorded there. This review does not certify exhaustive present openness.

sentences: The question asks whether every polynomially verifiable witness count can be evaluated exactly in deterministic polynomial time.
Witnesses are binary strings of a fixed polynomial length, and different witnesses retain their multiplicities.
The exact count is output in binary, so even an exponentially large value needs only polynomially many output bits.
An affirmative answer would imply P = NP, but efficient existence testing or relative approximation does not establish exact counting.
A resolution would settle the basic computational boundary for counting satisfiability, permanents and all other functions in #P.

cards.definitions:
Write \(\{0,1\}^*\) for all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) for their bit length. Natural numbers include zero. A polynomial witness bound is a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients; allowing any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded integer length gives the same class by unique zero padding. A verifier \(V(x,y)\) is a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine returning a bit on every pair of strings within polynomially many bit steps in \(|x|+|y|\). The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of the total functions
\[f_{V,p}(x)=\left|\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\right\}\right|.\]
Each distinct witness string is counted once. If several witnesses describe the same combinatorial object, their multiplicity is retained. The witness length is exactly the displayed length; shorter witnesses are not additionally counted. Equivalently, these functions count accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines with binary choices and an explicit machine convention preserving path counts.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to nonnegative integers for which some deterministic multitape Turing machine outputs the canonical binary representation on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps. Here \(C,d\) are fixed positive integers, the representation of zero is the single bit 0, and positive outputs have no leading zeros. All computation and output writing are charged. Machines have finite programs, no advice and no oracle. No error probability or approximation is allowed. The constants and program may depend on the function but never on the input. There is no requirement of a common exponent or a uniform compiler taking arbitrary verifiers as input.

Every \(\#\mathrm{P}\) value is at most \(2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has at most \(p(|x|)+1\) bits. The question does not request output in unary, listing all witnesses, or a time bound polynomial in the value of the count. Conversely, if a numerical function has a polynomial-time exact algorithm, choose a polynomial \(q\) longer than its output bit bound and accept a \(q(|x|)\)-bit witness precisely when its numerical value is smaller than \(f(x)\). Exactly \(f(x)\) witnesses are accepted. Thus \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm{P}\), which justifies writing equality rather than only the displayed inclusion. The source writes FP for this numerical interpretation of polynomial-time string functions.

For the comparisons below, \(\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages decided by deterministic machines in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages of the form \(\{x:f_{V,p}(x)>0\}\). Use the shared definition of [PSPACE](definitions.html#space). A polynomial-time Turing reduction to a numerical function may make adaptively chosen exact queries, charging query writing and answer processing, while receiving the binary answer from its oracle. Counting completeness mentioned below uses this convention unless a stronger count-preserving reduction is stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\), or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must supply existence of an exact uniform polynomial-time machine for every fixed verifier and witness bound; it suffices to solve an appropriately proved counting-complete problem exactly in polynomial time. A negative proof must establish a \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function admitting no such machine. A conditional separation assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), a lower bound for one restricted algorithm, or an efficient relative approximation does not by itself settle the unconditional proposition. Computing only whether the count is zero is also insufficient.

source_formulation.text: Can all #P functions be computed efficiently, so that FP and #P coincide under the binary-integer convention?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the explicit open question following Definition 9.2 in the January 2007 draft; numerical FP is made explicit.

context_blocks.text: A verifier checks one proposed witness quickly. Its counting function asks how many witnesses pass. The count can be exponentially large while its binary representation remains polynomially short, so the difficulty is not simply the time needed to write the answer.

Exact counting immediately decides whether any witness exists. Consequently, an affirmative answer implies P = NP, and a proof that P differs from NP would give a negative answer here. The converse implication is a separate question: efficient existence tests do not automatically evaluate the full count.

Counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is a representative complete problem. The usual verifier-to-formula construction can retain one satisfying assignment per accepted witness by forcing the values of auxiliary computation variables. Therefore a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm for those formulas would evaluate every function in the class.

Some counting-complete problems have easy existence tests. For a zero-one matrix, its permanent counts perfect matchings in the associated bipartite graph; testing whether such a matching exists is polynomial-time solvable. Counting completeness here is under polynomial-time oracle reductions, and does not mean a count-preserving reduction from satisfiability.

A polynomial-space computation can enumerate all witnesses while keeping only a polynomial-length counter. The textbook therefore notes that P = PSPACE would imply a positive answer. This stronger hypothesis is distinct from P = NP, and the brute-force counting procedure itself generally takes exponential time.

Relative approximation allows a nonzero error proportional to the count. When the count is exponential, even a very small inverse-polynomial relative error can hide many integers. An approximation algorithm whose running time is polynomial in inverse accuracy can need exponential time at the precision that distinguishes adjacent counts.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
cards.definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.
cards.why: Hadwiger’s conjecture proposes an exact relation between two basic graph parameters: the number of colors needed and the size of a complete graph obtainable by contraction. It extends the Four-Color Theorem and would turn exclusion of a complete minor into the sharp universal coloring bound. Its significance comes from this structural connection across all finite graphs, rather than from an algorithmic requirement in the question.

progress.text: Hadwiger’s original conjecture is restated in the introduction of the cited modern paper; the 1943 original was not inspected in this review.
Kostochka and Thomason establish the \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) degeneracy bound, summarized in Theorem 1.3 of Delcourt and Postle. Its tightness concerns degeneracy, not the conjectured chromatic bound.

Robertson, Seymour and Thomas establish the structural result that, with the Four-Color Theorem, proves five-colorability of \(K_6\)-minor-free graphs. The institutional abstract and publication metadata were checked.
Delcourt and Postle obtain \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors. The first preprint was submitted on 3 August 2021, the inspected version 5 on 5 March 2024, and the journal article appeared in 2025.

Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s Theorem 1.3 disproves the odd Hadwiger conjecture; their ordinary-minor Conjecture 1.1 remains a separate target. The preprint result is also cited in Liu and Luo’s September 2026 introduction.

Liu and Luo’s version 2 claims \(O(t\log\log\log t)\) colors in Theorem 1.1 and explicitly retains the ordinary Hadwiger conjecture as open. The arXiv version history still lists version 2 as latest on 14 September 2026; the proof was not independently verified.

references.title: Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture
references.authors: Marcus Kühn; Lisa Sauermann; Raphael Steiner; Yuval Wigderson
references.locator: Version 1, 23 December 2025; full PDF §1, ordinary Conjecture 1.1 on page 1, branch-tree odd-minor definition, Conjecture 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 on page 2. Still sole arXiv version on 14 September 2026; construction proof not independently certified.

cards.status_note: The ordinary Hadwiger conjecture is explicitly open in Liu–Luo v2 of 9 September 2026, still its latest arXiv version on 14 September. Its triple-logarithmic coloring theorem is a recent preprint claim, not independently verified here. The December 2025 disproof and its September 2026 citation concern the stronger odd-minor version. Checked source formulations and a bounded later-work search do not certify all cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: A complete minor can be much larger than any complete subgraph: contraction groups connected regions into single vertices. Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

cards.title: Deterministic Exact Matching
cards.formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with an even number \(n\ge0\) of vertices, every red-edge subset \(R\subseteq E\), and every integer \(0\le k\le n/2\), the machine halts within \(K(N+1)^d\) steps and outputs YES exactly when
\[
 \exists M\subseteq E:\qquad
 \bigl(\forall v\in V,\ |\{e\in M:v\in e\}|=1\bigr)
 \quad\text{and}\quad |M\cap R|=k?
\]
Here \(N\) is the input bit length under the explicit encoding below. No bipartition is promised.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated deterministic algorithm and common polynomial bound exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that this decision language does not belong to \(\mathrm{P}\).

A positive answer must cover both YES and NO instances on all finite simple graphs. A randomized polynomial-time procedure, nonuniform circuit family, special graph class, exact-parity test or algorithm with a small red-count or matching-size error does not by itself suffice. A conditional lower bound or a barrier to one algebraic approach is not an unconditional negative answer. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.
cards.why: Determine whether randomness can be removed from a basic exact constraint on perfect matching. The problem connects combinatorial derandomization with algebraic algorithms while keeping a short, directly checkable input and feasibility condition.
cards.definitions:
Vertices are labelled \(1,\ldots,n\), and an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Loops and parallel edges are excluded. Every edge is either red, meaning it belongs to \(R\), or blue, meaning it belongs to \(E\setminus R\). The graph, all its edges and their colours are given explicitly, not through an oracle or a succinct circuit. One fixed encoding uses a length-prefixed binary header and a list of adjacency records, one for each vertex including isolated vertices, with neighbour labels and colour bits; each undirected edge has consistent entries at both endpoints. The integer \(k\) is in binary. The encoding contains all \(n\) vertex records, so its length is at least \(n\); a binary header alone does not describe exponentially many unlisted vertices.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to one of its edges, equivalently the degree condition in the formula. Every perfect matching then has \(n/2\) edges. The requested count is exactly \(k\) red edges, rather than at least \(k\), at most \(k\) or a count congruent to \(k\) modulo an integer. On the empty graph, the empty matching is perfect and the allowed input \(k=0\) has answer YES.

The machine is one uniform finite classical multitape Turing program; all bit operations, reading, auxiliary computation and output count toward its running time. It has no random bits, nonuniform advice or external oracle. The same \(A,K,d\) must work on every input size, colour pattern and allowed \(k\), with no error. Malformed encodings, odd vertex counts and out-of-range values of \(k\) can be rejected as invalid inputs in polynomial time. The graph may be disconnected, nonplanar and nonbipartite, with arbitrary degrees.

The required output is a decision bit; computing the number of matchings is not requested. Polynomial time means membership of this explicitly encoded decision language in the class \(\mathrm{P}\). Only sequential polynomial time is sought; a polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithm is not required. The statement is unconditional: no computational hardness or derandomization assumption is supplied.

context_blocks.text: An ordinary perfect matching covers every vertex once. The exact colour constraint asks for one specified attainable count, which is not determined merely by optimizing the count upward or downward.

On a six-cycle whose edge colours alternate red and blue, the two perfect matchings have zero and three red edges. Counts one and two are absent even though they lie between the minimum and maximum. This elementary obstruction already occurs on bipartite inputs.

Randomized methods place the problem among natural candidates for studying the power of randomness in efficient computation. A matching witnesses a YES answer, but the target requires a deterministic polynomial-time decision on NO instances as well.

The August 2026 revision tests all red counts simultaneously in matrix-multiplication time measured in finite-field operations. Its decision algorithm still uses randomness, and the introduction explicitly leaves derandomization open.

The April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic algorithm only for bipartite graphs. Its Appendix A records eight unproved structural inputs in the Lean formalization. This review does not certify those inputs or the full proof; even a verified bipartite theorem would require a further general-graph argument to settle this card.

cards.context:
An ordinary perfect matching covers every vertex once. The exact colour constraint asks for one specified attainable count, which is not determined merely by optimizing the count upward or downward.

On a six-cycle whose edge colours alternate red and blue, the two perfect matchings have zero and three red edges. Counts one and two are absent even though they lie between the minimum and maximum. This elementary obstruction already occurs on bipartite inputs.

Randomized methods place the problem among natural candidates for studying the power of randomness in efficient computation. A matching witnesses a YES answer, but the target requires a deterministic polynomial-time decision on NO instances as well.

The August 2026 revision tests all red counts simultaneously in matrix-multiplication time measured in finite-field operations. Its decision algorithm still uses randomness, and the introduction explicitly leaves derandomization open.

The April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic algorithm only for bipartite graphs. Its Appendix A records eight unproved structural inputs in the Lean formalization. This review does not certify those inputs or the full proof; even a verified bipartite theorem would require a further general-graph argument to settle this card.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.
Tango trees give an online BST with an \(O(\log\log n)\) competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying.
The preprint proves \(O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

cards.status_note: Uncertain after review on 15 September 2026. The inspected October 2025 preprint, published at SODA 2026, explicitly leaves the deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case target open and proves an expected randomized bound plus a conditional deterministic theorem. However, the official FOCS 2026 accepted list and an author page now announce a closely matching new paper by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Yeh. The inspected listings contain no theorem statement or manuscript link; bounded searches did not obtain its full text. Its determinism, error guarantee and exact model therefore remain unchecked. The card stays active with a complete formulation, without treating an announcement title as a matching solution or asserting current openness from the older source.

context_blocks.text: Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

cards.context:
Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

cards.title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed real deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), do there exist constants \(C_\delta>0\) and \(a_\delta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that \[N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta n^{a_\delta}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge2?\] Here \(N_\delta(n)\), defined below, is the number of independent deletion traces needed to reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with success probability at least \(2/3\). Processing is unrestricted, and the length and deletion probability are known. Constants may depend on fixed \(\delta\).
cards.definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each fixed deletion probability the worst-case trace count for exact reconstruction at success probability \(2/3\) is polynomial in the string length. A refutation requires one fixed deletion probability for which no polynomial bound suffices.
cards.why: Determine the intrinsic amount of information needed to recover an arbitrary string when repeated observations lose the positions of deleted symbols. This separates the statistical cost of hidden alignment from the computational cost of processing the observations.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected July 2026 preprint gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for every fixed retention probability, while the unrestricted lower bound cited by it and the September graph-trace preprint remains polynomial. The cited quasipolynomial upper and polynomial lower bounds alone do not decide whether polynomially many traces suffice. context_blocks.text: The selected binary target asks whether a polynomial number of traces suffices for every fixed deletion rate. It does not require the optimal sample exponent or a polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its bound is \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\), for retention probability \(p=1-\delta\) and an absolute constant \(c\). This dated theorem does not by itself give a polynomial bound.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

cards.title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?

cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent two
cards.formal: Does the matrix multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\) equal two? Precisely, writing \(s(n)\) for the minimum arithmetic gate count of an exact circuit multiplying two \(n\times n\) complex matrices, is it true that \[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2},\qquad s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}?\] The circuit family and its constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\); an \(O(n^2)\) bound is not required.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required \(n^2\) outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). Use an [arithmetic circuit](definitions.html#arithmetic-circuits) over \(\mathbb C\), with input variables, arbitrary field constants, and binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position \((i,j)\) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly \(c_{ij}\), so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The binary target is \(\omega=2\), with the positive-slack convention just stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an upper bound \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\) on the specified arithmetic-circuit size over \(\mathbb C\), or show that some positive \(\varepsilon\) admits no such bound.

progress.text: Strassen gives matrix multiplication in \(O(n^{\log_2 7})\) arithmetic operations, establishing a strictly subcubic exponent.
Alman’s revised universal-method paper proves that its application to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot give an exponent below 2.16805. This is a method-specific barrier.
The SODA publication of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication states \(\omega<2.371339\).

Dupont and coauthors report \(\omega<2.371177\). Section 4 describes rational certification and says the verification repository is being prepared; that certificate has not been replayed in this review.
The third arXiv revision of More Asymmetry incorporates the later optimization while distinguishing it from the original published bound. It does not establish a matching general lower bound.

cards.status_note: The checked source states the exponent-two conjecture, and the August 2026 papers report improved upper bounds without determining omega. Those upper bounds do not establish the exponent-two assertion selected here. The recorded source search was bounded and took place on 14 September 2026. The optimization certificate was not independently replayed, and its repository was still described as in preparation in the checked version.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The selected target is the familiar conjecture \(\omega=2\). Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, a separate circuit family and constant are permitted for every positive slack in the exponent. This is weaker than requiring an \(O(n^2)\) circuit-size bound and is distinct from numerical approximation of the exponent.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An upper bound strictly above two does not by itself settle this binary question. Conversely, a negative answer must prove \(\omega>2\) for unrestricted circuits, rather than a barrier for one tensor framework.
